provenance: Synthetic parser/framing conformance oracle for ContextDesk. Every fixture byte is derived from public format documentation (PostgreSQL log_line_prefix/csvlog/jsonlog, RFC3339, RFC5424, logfmt, and the standard exception renderings of the JVM, .NET, Python, Rust, and Go). No customer, employer, production, or developer-machine material, no credentials, no private paths, and no evaluator answer keys. Corpus is emitted by scripts/generate_conformance_corpus.py; expectations are driven through the real ingest pipeline by crates/cd-core/tests/log_conformance.rs.

statuses.holds: Behavior is already correct on main. Asserted directly; a regression fails the default suite.
statuses.gap: A known failure. `desired` states what production must eventually produce; `observed` records exactly what main produces today. The default suite asserts `observed`, so CI stays green and the gap cannot be silently weakened into a pass -- when production improves, the quarantine fails and forces an explicit reclassification.

invariant_note: Cases marked `invariant: true` must hold in every state, before and after any gap is repaired. They are the properties a framing or grammar change is most likely to break: no record may be dropped, no wall clock may be fabricated, source identity must stay distinct, and a false continuation must never be merged.

assertions.record_count: Number of logical records the import produced for this input.
assertions.record_field: Locate the single record whose message contains `where_contains`, then compare `field`. The pseudo-field `message_chars` compares the message length.
assertions.sources: Sorted distinct source identities produced by the import.

cases.title: DETAIL/HINT/STATEMENT belong to the ERROR they follow
cases.note: PostgreSQL emits one logical server message as a primary line plus indented-or-tagged continuation lines sharing the same pid and timestamp. Six physical lines are three logical records: the startup LOG, the ERROR with its DETAIL/HINT/STATEMENT, and the checkpoint LOG.

cases.title: %m with an unambiguous UTC abbreviation is a wall clock
cases.note: `2025-06-15 12:00:00.123 UTC` names a zone that has exactly one meaning, so it is an instant rather than order-only evidence. There is no PostgreSQL grammar today, so the whole line falls back to plain text.

cases.title: PostgreSQL LOG severity is not `unknown`
cases.note: LOG is a real PostgreSQL severity. It currently survives nowhere because no grammar reads the severity tag and the plain-text token scan only recognizes DEBUG/INFO/WARN/ERROR/FATAL/TRACE.

cases.title: An ERROR row is never classified below error
cases.note: Holds today only because the plain-text token scan happens to find the ERROR tag. It is listed as an invariant so a future grammar cannot regress it.

cases.title: An ambiguous zone abbreviation never becomes an instant
cases.note: CST is North American or Chinese depending on deployment. No amount of grammar work may turn this into a wall clock without an explicit source timezone policy.

cases.title: The local calendar text should still be retained as evidence
cases.note: Refusing to resolve is correct; discarding the evidence is not. The local portion is a complete calendar time and should be retained so an explicit timezone policy can resolve it later.

cases.title: Rotated files keep distinct identities despite overlapping time
A newline inside a quoted CSV field does not end the record
cases.note: The documented csvlog contract quotes every text field and permits embedded newlines in `query`/`message`/`detail`. Three logical rows currently arrive as five records, and the two fragments carry no timestamp, severity, or session identity at all.

cases.title: `VALUES (42, 'demo')` is a fragment, not an event
cases.note: A continuation fragment presented as a standalone event is false evidence: it carries no time, no severity, and no session. Counting records alone would not catch a framer that merged the wrong lines, so this case checks that the fragment ends up inside the ERROR row it belongs to.

cases.title: One JSON object per line is one record
The documented `message` field becomes the message

cases.title: jsonlog `timestamp` is a documented field with an unambiguous zone
cases.note: The value is `2025-06-15 12:20:05.250 UTC`. The alias is found, but the text is neither RFC3339 nor a bare local datetime, so it is discarded entirely and the row becomes order-only.

cases.title: jsonlog carries severity in `error_severity`, not `level`
cases.note: A schema-specific mapping must run before the generic alias list, or every PostgreSQL jsonlog row is severity-less.

cases.note: Refusing to resolve it is right. Discarding it means an explicit source-timezone policy can never recover the row.

cases.title: A bare `20250615` must not be accepted as epoch seconds
cases.note: The integer 20250615 lands inside the epoch-seconds band [0, 1e11) and is accepted as an instant, producing 1970-08-23 and marking it explicit_wall_clock. This is a fabricated wall clock from a date-shaped integer -- the most serious class of error this lab exists to catch, because the row then sorts, filters, and renders as real calendar time. No listed issue covers it.

cases.title: The fabricated instant lands in 1970
cases.note: Pins the concrete wrong value so the repair is unambiguous: 20250615 seconds after the epoch is 1970-08-23T02:03:35Z.

cases.title: Serilog's `@t` timestamp alias is not recognized
The `eventTime` alias is not recognized
A span id is not a trace id
cases.note: `span_id` sits in the trace_id alias list, so a record carrying only a span is reported as if it carried a trace. Correlating on that value groups unrelated events.

cases.title: A request id is retained as its own correlation, not as a trace
An explicit trace id wins over a span id
TRACE is not DEBUG
CRITICAL is not FATAL
An unrecognized vocabulary term survives verbatim
cases.note: Holds today because normalize_level passes unknown terms through lowercased rather than flattening them to `unknown`.

cases.title: A numeric Pino level is severity evidence
cases.note: Pino encodes error as 50. The alias lookup only accepts strings, so every numeric-level producer arrives severity-less.

cases.title: "no errors detected" is not an error
cases.note: The JSON path does not infer severity from message text. The syslog path does, using a bare substring scan, so this invariant guards against that inference spreading.

cases.title: logfmt `ts=` with RFC3339 is an instant
logfmt offsetless local time is retained as evidence
logfmt `timestamp=` with a numeric epoch is not decoded
cases.note: The JSON path decodes epoch units; the logfmt path does not, so the same value is an instant in one format and order-only in the other.

cases.title: A JVM stack trace with a cause and a suppressed frame is one record
cases.note: Ten physical lines are two logical events: the failed submission with its whole trace, and the retry notice.

cases.title: `Caused by:` is not a standalone event
cases.note: The cause belongs to the ERROR that raised it. Today it is its own severity-less record, so the chain that explains the failure is split away from the failure.

cases.title: A Kotlin coroutine trace with a cause is one record
A .NET trace with an inner exception is one record
A chained Python traceback with blank separators is one record
cases.note: The blank lines inside the chained traceback are part of the record. They are currently skipped outright, so the framer must not treat a blank line as a terminator.

cases.title: A Rust panic with a backtrace is one record
A Go panic with goroutine frames is one record
Indentation and the words `Caused by:` do not make a continuation
cases.note: The adversary: one record legitimately contains the text `Caused by:` in its message, and one genuinely new record is indented. A framer keying on leading whitespace or that substring alone will merge them and destroy two real events. This must stay four before and after framing lands.

cases.title: Truncated JSON falls back to the whole line as the message
A non-scalar timestamp is unusable, not guessed
A duplicated `ts` key silently takes the last value
cases.note: The record carries `ts` twice. The later value wins with no warning, so a trailing duplicate can move an event nearly twelve hours. #789 requires duplicate keys to fail safely with an explicit warning; parse warnings are not observable through the event API yet, so this case pins the current silent behavior.
